head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dict timestamp → the CURRENT price for it (corrections overwrite)
A max-heap (stored as negated prices) and a min-heap of (price, timestamp) pairs; every update is pushed, even for a corrected timestamp
An entry is stale if its price no longer equals the dict's price for that timestamp; stale entries are discarded only when they reach the top
Peek at the largest price (the heap root)

p: The sequence from the problem; the last column is the size of the max-heap, including stale entries:

A heap cannot remove an arbitrary entry cheaply when a timestamp is corrected. Instead the old entry stays and is recognised as stale (it disagrees with `prices`) when it surfaces. Each entry is popped at most once, so the total cost stays O(log n) amortized per operation.

bullets: `update`: O(log n). `maximum`/`minimum`: O(log n) amortized. `current`: O(1).
Space: O(n) including stale heap entries.

2034.takeaway: Dict of current prices plus two heaps with lazy deletion of stale entries.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Range of possible products (values up to 10⁵ each, so products up to 10¹⁰)
Binary search on the answer value
How many pairs (a, b) have a · b ≤ v, found per `a` with a binary search in the sorted nums2
a·b ≤ v ⇔ b ≤ floor(v / a) for positive a
Floor division works for negative v too
Dividing by a negative a reverses the inequality: b ≥ ceil(v / a), so count elements from that position to the end
The product is 0: it is ≤ v when v ≥ 0 (all m pairs count), otherwise none
Smallest v with at least k pairs ≤ v is the k-th smallest product

p: `nums1 = [2,5]`, `nums2 = [3,4]`, k = 2. The products are 6, 8, 15, 20. `count(v)` for a few values:
bullets: The smallest v with count(v) ≥ 2 is 8 (after 34 halvings).

p: Multiplying an inequality by a negative number flips it, so the matching elements of nums2 are those at the END of the sorted array, not the start. That is why the negative branch counts `m - bisect_left(...)` and uses ceiling-style division.

bullets: Time: O(n · log m · log(range)): about 35 halvings of the value range, each with n binary searches.

2040.takeaway: Binary search on the product value; count pairs ≤ v with one bisect per element, flipping the direction for negatives.

head: Code

Validates that the account number exists (1 to n)
not (ok1 and ok2) or bal < money → False
Validate both accounts before touching either balance, and check funds
The transfer itself, done only after all checks passed so there is no partial update

p: A failed transfer must leave both balances unchanged. If the withdrawal were done first and then account 2 found invalid, money would vanish. Checking account numbers and the available balance first guarantees all-or-nothing behaviour.

2043.takeaway: Validate accounts and funds first, then mutate balances; account numbers are 1-based.

What it does

Number of nodes in u's subtree, computed by post-order DFS (Depth-First Search): `1 + sum(go(v) …)`
Removing u leaves its child subtrees and the rest of the tree (n − size[u], if not empty); the score is the product of their sizes
Track the maximum score and how many nodes reach it

bullets: Highest score 4 is reached by 3 nodes.

p: Deleting node u splits the tree into its children's subtrees plus the remainder above it. The sizes of these components are all the score needs, and every size comes from one DFS.

bullets: Space: O(n); the recursion is as deep as the tree.

2049.takeaway: One DFS for subtree sizes; each node's score is the product of its children's sizes and n − size.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Prefix sum: number of plates `*` among the first i + 1 characters
Index of the first candle at or after i (n if none)
Index of the last candle at or before i (−1 if none)
At least two distinct candles inside the query; plates between them count
Plates strictly between the leftmost candle `a` and the rightmost candle `b`

blocks.h: Why trim to the outermost candles?
p: Plates only count if they lie between two candles that are both inside the query range. Plates before the first candle or after the last candle in the range don't have a candle on one side, so the query is shrunk to [first candle, last candle] first.

bullets: Time: O(n + q) with precomputation and O(1) per query.

2055.takeaway: Prefix sums of plates plus nearest-candle arrays: shrink each query to its outermost candles, then subtract prefixes.

Letter counts in the current window

Walk along unused edges; when stuck, pop the node onto `path`
Nodes pop in reverse order of the trail

blocks.h: Why does Hierholzer produce a valid trail?
p: When the walk gets stuck, the stuck node is the last node of the trail (it has no unused edges). Placing it first into `path` and then backtracking splices in any detours. After the final reversal, every edge appears exactly once in a connected order.

2097.takeaway: Hierholzer's algorithm for a directed Euler path, starting at the node with out-degree minus in-degree equal to 1.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: How many distinct ingredients are still missing (a set removes duplicates)
Kahn's algorithm (topological order by counting unmet prerequisites)
Start from what we already have
An ingredient arrived; when none is missing the recipe can be made, and it then becomes an ingredient itself

p: Recipes `bread` (yeast, flour) and `sandwich` (bread, meat); supplies yeast, flour, meat:

blocks.h: Why does a cycle or missing ingredient cause no output for that recipe?
p: A recipe is added only when its missing count reaches 0. Recipes in a cycle wait for each other forever, and recipes needing an unavailable ingredient never reach 0, so they are never reported.

bullets: Time: O(V + E) over recipes and ingredient links.

2115.takeaway: Topological sort (Kahn): ingredients arrive, recipes whose missing count reaches 0 become new ingredients.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Copies the list's values into an array so we can index from both ends
The mirror element of vals[i] from the end (index −1 is the last)
Only the first half; each twin pair is visited once

p: `4 → 2 → 2 → 3`: node i and node n−1−i are twins.

blocks.h: Why an array and not pointers?
p: A singly linked list can't be walked from the end. Copying to an array costs O(n) space but is simple. The O(1)-space alternative reverses the second half in place (after finding the middle with slow/fast pointers) and walks both halves together.

2130.takeaway: Copy values to a list and pair index i with n−1−i; the O(1)-space version reverses the second half.

What it does

rows: Pairs each seed's (grow, plant) and orders by growing time, longest first
Sorting by one key of a tuple
Planting is sequential: you can plant only one seed at a time, so `t` is the day planting finishes
That seed blooms after its growing time
The full bloom day is when the last seed blooms

p: `plantTime = [1,4,3]`, `growTime = [2,3,1]`; seeds in order of decreasing grow time:

blocks.h: Why plant the slowest-growing seeds first?
p: Planting happens one after another, but growing overlaps. Starting the long-growing seeds early lets their long growth overlap with the planting of the others. An exchange argument shows that putting a seed with a smaller grow time before a larger one never helps.

2136.takeaway: Plant in order of decreasing grow time so long growth overlaps with other planting.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: The hidden sequence relative to its first element (first = 0)
The lowest and highest values reached by that relative sequence (both include the starting 0)
The first element can slide over a window of size (upper − lower + 1) − (hi − lo): each choice must keep the whole sequence in [lower, upper]
If the spread hi − lo is too big, no start works

p: `differences = [1,-3,4]`, range [1, 6]:
bullets: Spread 4; choices for the first value: (6 − 1) − (2 − (-2)) + 1 = 2.

blocks.h: Why does only the spread matter?
p: Choosing the first element s shifts the whole sequence by s. It fits in [lower, upper] iff s + lo ≥ lower and s + hi ≤ upper, i.e. s in [lower − lo, upper − hi]. The number of integers in that interval is (upper − hi) − (lower − lo) + 1 = (upper − lower) − (hi − lo) + 1.

2145.takeaway: Hidden sequences correspond to valid starts; the count is range size minus the sequence's spread (max − min).

bullets: Right side (scanning right to left, sum of the 2 largest of the suffix):

p: Answer: 1.

blocks.h: Why two heaps and a split point?
p: After removing n elements, the remaining 2n elements split into a first half (from the left part) and a second half. For a split point i, the best choice is the n smallest from the prefix and the n largest from the suffix. Precomputing all prefix and suffix values with heaps takes O(n log n) for all split points.

2163.takeaway: Two sweeps with heaps: smallest-n prefix sums from the left, largest-n suffix sums from the right; minimize the difference over split points.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Both must be non-zero to continue
Subtract the smaller from the larger

p: Subtraction can take many steps when one number is much larger. Division gives the same count in O(log) time: `ops += num1 // num2` then `num1 %= num2` (and swap roles). The subtraction version is fine for the problem's limit of 10⁵.

bullets: Time: O(max(num1, num2)) in the worst case.

2169.takeaway: Subtractive Euclid: subtract the smaller from the larger, counting steps until one is zero.

Moving the partner from index i to index 0 takes i adjacent swaps; the real implementation just removes it, charging i moves

blocks.h: Why match the last character with its first occurrence?
p: To make the outermost pair equal, the right end needs a partner on the left. The nearest-to-the-front copy is the cheapest to bring: moving it costs i swaps, while choosing a later copy would also be fine but the first copy keeps the other copies in place for later pairs. This greedy is optimal.

bullets: Time: O(n²) (index and pop are O(n), repeated n/2 times).

2193.takeaway: Greedy from the outside: pair the last character with its first occurrence, paying its index in adjacent swaps.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Value → TreeNode, created on first mention so a node is shared between its parent and child roles
Links the child using the flag (1 = left, 0 = right)
Records every value that appears as a child
The root is the only node that is never a child
Finding the root of a tree from parent links

bullets: The only value never a child is 50: the root. Tree: `50(20(15,17),80(19,))`.

blocks.h: Why a shared dict of nodes?
p: Descriptions arrive in any order, and a node appears both as a child (in one row) and as a parent (in others). Using one dict guarantees both roles refer to the same object, so the links connect up regardless of order.

2196.takeaway: Create nodes on demand in a dict, link by the left/right flag, and the root is the one value never used as a child.
